summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for carrying Video Codec 1 (VC-1) streams, defined by the SMPTE 421M standard for television. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: A video format needs a way to be cut into pieces and sent over the internet live. This explains how to do that for one such format.

questions: what is the rtp payload format for vc-1
how is vc-1 fragmented in rtp
what is the sdp media type for vc-1
what is the au header in vc-1 rtp
subtitle: How to chop VC-1 compressed video into RTP packets and describe it in SDP.

tldr.problem: VC-1 is a video compression format standardized as SMPTE 421M, but it defines only the bit stream, not how to carry it in RTP packets over an IP network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4425 packs VC-1 data into Access Units with a small AU header, fragments large frames to fit the MTU, sets RTP timestamps from presentation times, and defines the video/vc1 media type and its SDP parameters.
tldr.outcome: Senders and receivers can stream VC-1 over RTP and negotiate profile, level and size limits in SDP. Users must also follow congestion control rules because streams can need very high bandwidth.

today: RFC 4425 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the VC-1 RTP payload format.

sections.title: What This Payload Format Does
sections.content:
RFC 4425 specifies an RTP payload format for Video Codec 1 (VC-1), the compressed video bit stream defined by the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE) in standard SMPTE 421M. That standard defines the bit stream syntax and the decoding process for television, but it does not specify the compression algorithm, so different encoders are possible.

The RFC says VC-1 suits uses ranging from low bit rate Internet streaming to High Definition Television (HDTV) broadcast and Digital Cinema, and that it is used in the form of Windows Media Video 9 (WMV-9) and adopted for HD DVD and Blu-ray. These are claims the document makes about VC-1, and this RFC itself only defines how to carry the bits in RTP.
sections.eli5: VC-1 is a way to squash video so it takes less space. This document is about the delivery truck that carries the squashed video across the internet.

sections.title: VC-1 in Brief
sections.content:
The VC-1 bit stream has three profiles: Simple, Main and Advanced. Simple is for low bit rates and low complexity, with a maximum of 384 kbps. Main targets high bit rate uses such as streaming and TV over IP and adds B-pictures. Advanced supports interlaced video, non-square pixels, in-band user-data and in-band changes of codec parameters, and a maximum of 135 Mbps. Each profile has levels: two for Simple, three for Main and five for Advanced.

The stream is a hierarchy of layers: sequence, entry-point, picture, slice, macroblock and block. Entry-point and slice layers exist only in Advanced profile. In Advanced profile each picture and slice is a bit-stream data unit (BDU) that begins with a four-byte start code: 0x00, 0x00, 0x01 and a suffix byte that gives the BDU type. To stop the start code appearing by accident, SMPTE 421M uses byte stuffing; a stuffed BDU is an EBDU.

Frames are sent in coded order. When B-pictures are present, the frames they depend on are sent first, so the display order differs from the order in which frames are sent and the decoder must hold one extra frame.
sections.eli5: VC-1 comes in small, medium and large sizes. The big one can handle fancy TV pictures. Some pictures need to be sent early because later pictures lean on them, like laying a floor before the rug.

sections.title: Access Units and Fragmentation
sections.content:
Each RTP packet holds one or more Access Units (AUs). An AU is an AU header followed by a payload, and the payload MUST contain data from exactly one VC-1 frame. A frame may be split across several AUs, but two frames never share an AU. For Advanced profile the payload MUST be in EBDU format and MUST start at an EBDU boundary (unless it is a later fragment); for Simple and Main it MUST start at the beginning of a frame. AUs MUST be byte-aligned, with up to 7 zero padding bits if needed.

Each AU payload SHOULD hold a complete frame. If that would make the RTP packet exceed the MTU, the frame SHOULD be fragmented to avoid IP-level fragmentation, and the FRAG field in the AU header MUST say so. For a later fragment in Advanced profile, starting at an EBDU boundary such as a slice is preferred, and a receiver can check by looking for the start code prefix 0x00 0x00 0x01. In Simple and Main profiles the split point can be arbitrary. After the last fragment of a frame, further AUs SHOULD NOT be added to the packet.

The marker bit is set to 1 when the packet contains a complete frame or the last fragment of a frame.
sections.eli5: If a picture is too big for one envelope, it is split over several envelopes. Each envelope holds only pieces of one picture, and the last piece is marked.

sections.title: The AU Header
sections.content:
The AU header is a one-byte AU Control field, an 8-bit RA Count field and three optional fields, all in network byte order. AUP Len (16 bits) gives the payload size and MUST be present in every AU header in a packet except the last. PTS Delta (32 bits) is a signed offset from the RTP timestamp to the frame's presentation time, and DTS Delta (32 bits) is the offset between presentation time and decode time.

The AU Control bits are FRAG (2 bits), RA, SL, LP, PT, DT and R (1 bit each). LP, PT and DT say whether AUP Len, PTS Delta and DTS Delta are present. R is reserved, MUST be 0 and MUST be ignored by receivers. RA marks a random access point. SL toggles when a different sequence layer header is sent.
sections.eli5: Each piece has a small label: is it the first piece, the middle or the last, is this a good place to start watching, and how long is it.

sections.title: Timing, Random Access and Headers
sections.content:
Frames MUST be sent in coded order. The RTP timestamp MUST be set to the presentation time of the frame in the first AU, using a 90 kHz clock. If another AU in the packet has a different presentation time, that time MUST be given with PTS Delta. The decode time equals the presentation time unless B-pictures may be present, in which case the RFC gives rules for B-frames and non-B frames and requires DTS Delta whenever decode and presentation times differ. Receivers are not required to use DTS Delta.

The first frame after an entry-point header is a random access point; in Simple and Main profiles every I-picture is one. The RA Count field increments modulo 256 for each AU with the RA bit set, so a receiver can tell whether a lost packet held a random access point.

Advanced profile sequence headers can carry up to 31 leaky bucket parameter sets for the Hypothetical Reference Decoder. A sender that knows the real peak rate MAY remove all but one, and MUST then also remove the matching HRD_FULL values in the entry-point header. If the sequence layer header changes, it is RECOMMENDED to repeat it often for robustness.

When the media type parameter mode is 1, the sequence layer header never changes and the sender MAY drop it. With mode=3, neither the sequence layer header nor the entry-point header changes, so both may be left out; the receiver MUST re-insert the entry-point header from the config parameter when an AU has the RA bit set but does not begin with one.
sections.eli5: Every piece carries a clock reading so the video plays at the right moment. A counter on the good starting points lets the viewer notice when one went missing.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type video/vc1. In SDP, the encoding name is vc1, the clock rate MUST be 90000, and the parameters go in an a=fmtp line as semicolon-separated name=value pairs. Unknown parameters MUST be ignored.

profile (0 Simple, 1 Main, 3 Advanced) and level are required. Optional parameters are config (a base16 octet string of decoder initialization parameters), width, height, bitrate, buffer, framerate (frames per second times 1000, so 29.97 is 29970), bpic and mode. The max-width, max-height, max-bitrate, max-buffer and max-framerate parameters express receiver capabilities or preferences.

In the SDP Offer/Answer model, profile is used symmetrically, and an answerer MUST NOT specify a numerically higher level than the offer, though it may downgrade it. For multicast, the answerer MUST NOT change these values and can only accept or remove the payload type. In declarative uses such as RTSP or SAP, config, width, height, bitrate and buffer MUST be given and the max- parameters MUST NOT be used.
sections.eli5: Before the show starts, the sender hands over a fact sheet: what kind of video, how big the picture is, and how fast the data flows, so the receiver can get ready.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Packets are subject to the security considerations of RTP and the RTP profile in use, so confidentiality comes from encryption such as SRTP. The RFC warns of a denial-of-service threat: an attacker can inject pathological packets that are costly to decode, and VC-1 is particularly vulnerable because frames can affect the decoding of many future frames. Data origin authentication and integrity protection of at least the RTP packet are therefore RECOMMENDED.

VC-1 can also carry user-data such as closed captions. Its interpretation is not defined by VC-1, and malformed user-data might crash a receiver. Senders SHOULD make sure user-data complies with what is registered with SMPTE, and receivers SHOULD prevent malfunction on non-compliant user-data.
sections.eli5: A bad guy could mail you a puzzle that takes forever to solve and jams your desk. Checking who really sent each envelope helps keep that out.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content:
Because VC-1 streams can need up to 135 Mbps, users of this format MUST follow RTP congestion control (RFC 3550 and the applicable profile). On best-effort networks, loss is acceptable only if a TCP flow on the same path would get at least the average throughput the RTP flow is getting. Senders can meet this by adapting the rate, or by having a receiver leave the session when loss is too high.

For pre-encoded content, adaptation needs more than one coded representation at different bit rates, switched at random access points, or non-reference frames such as B-frames that can be discarded before packetizing. The result MUST still comply with VC-1, so counters such as FRMCNT and TFCNTR must still count discarded frames. Only a change of a non-downgradable parameter such as profile forces the stream to restart, for instance with a new payload type.
sections.eli5: If the road is jammed, send fewer cars. A sender can send a smaller version of the video, or skip the pictures nobody depends on.

fields.name: FRAG
fields.desc: Whether the payload holds a complete frame or a fragment.

fields.name: RA
fields.desc: Set when the AU contains a random access point.

fields.name: SL
fields.desc: Toggled when a changed sequence layer header is sent.

fields.name: LP
fields.desc: Set when the AUP Len field is present.

fields.name: PT
fields.desc: Set when the PTS Delta field is present.

fields.name: DT
fields.desc: Set when the DTS Delta field is present.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved; must be 0 and ignored by receivers.

items.label: Middle fragment
items.desc: A fragment of a frame other than the first or last.

items.label: First fragment
items.desc: The first fragment of a frame.

items.label: Last fragment
items.desc: The last fragment of a frame.

items.label: Complete frame
items.desc: The payload holds a whole, unfragmented frame.
